title: Why the Roman Republic fell
hook: For nearly 500 years the Romans refused to let any one man rule them. Then, in little more than a century, they ended up with an emperor. What went wrong?
oneBreath: Rome's Republic was designed so that no one could become king: power was shared between officials elected for a year, a Senate of former officials and assemblies of citizens. Conquest made Rome rich but strained that system, as land, armies and politics came to depend on a few ambitious generals, until civil wars ended with Augustus ruling behind a republican front. Historians still argue about which pressures mattered most.

ideas.title: Power that expires: two consuls, one year
ideas.oneLine: Rome replaced its kings with two consuls elected for one year at a time, each able to block the other.

ideas.title: Senate, assemblies and tribunes
ideas.oneLine: Who really decided things: a Senate of former officials advised, citizen assemblies voted, and tribunes could veto on behalf of ordinary people.

ideas.title: Conquest's side effects: wealth, slaves and land
ideas.oneLine: Winning an empire flooded Rome with wealth and enslaved people, and many small farmers struggled, though historians debate how badly.

ideas.title: The Gracchi: when politics turned violent
ideas.oneLine: Two brothers pushed land reforms as tribunes in 133 and 123 BC, and both were killed, teaching Roman politics to use force.

ideas.title: Armies loyal to their generals
ideas.oneLine: Why soldiers came to follow commanders who could reward them, and why historians still argue about how much Marius changed.

ideas.title: Sulla and Caesar march on Rome
ideas.oneLine: Twice in forty years a general led his army against his own government, and the Republic's rules could not stop him.

ideas.title: Augustus: a republic in name only
ideas.oneLine: Augustus kept the old offices and the Senate but held the real power, and that is why his rule lasted where Caesar's did not.

calibration.q: A new law was about to be voted on in a Roman assembly when a single tribune stood up and said "I forbid it". What happened next?
options: The vote went ahead: one man could not stop a whole assembly
The Senate met to decide whether he could object
calibration.why: The vote was stopped. One tribune's veto could halt it, however many citizens wanted the law: a power meant to protect ordinary people from the powerful.

calibration.q: By the first century BC, why did Roman soldiers often side with their general against the government?
options: They were foreign mercenaries with no loyalty to Rome
Their general, not the state, was their best hope of land or reward
The law said soldiers must obey their general over the Senate
calibration.why: Many soldiers were poor citizens who looked to their commander to win them land or money when they left the army, so their loyalty leaned towards him. They were Roman citizens, not foreign mercenaries.
